blocks.x: Director Mike Leigh‘s filmography is full of intricate personal dramas driven by idiosyncratic characters coping with everyday troubles. The emotional climaxes of his movies mostly spill over the dinner table or a conversation on the couch, giving his actors the full range to fill up the screen with their nuanced performances. Whether it’s making the decision to find one’s biological parents in Secret And Lies, or pointing out how people struggle to accept someone else’s happiness in Happy-Go-Lucky, Leigh crafts each story with great attention to the relationships holding them together, continuing to pry into kitchen-sink dramas and lighthearted domestic comedies to find both the good, with movies like Vera Drake, and the difficult, as seen in Hard Truths, in humanity. Tender Loving Care, which Leigh claims will be his final film, weaves these same emotional threads into another subtle but moving slice-of-life tapestry.

Exploring the different kinds of emotional labor at work and in the home, Tender Loving Care highlights its characters’ different caregiving roles, from doting parents to dealing with difficult cases on the job. Leigh shows how much work it takes to be there for one another, and how deeply people support those they care about. In quiet moments, Leigh and his actors say so much just by quietly being present for their loved ones and the people they’re charged with helping.

After a long-troubled relationship finally comes to the end, Amy (Widow’s Bay breakout Kate O’Flynn) returns to her old flat, and her roommate Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson) is only happy to welcome her back. The pair are longtime friends who swap dating horror stories and vent their work stresses. While Rosie is excited about a new romantic prospect with a fireman, Amy is reluctant to break her relationship news to her parents, Birdie (Marion Bailey) and Geoff (Paul Jesson), since they fret over their daughter’s chances of finding a decent partner. However, when Geoff starts presenting concerning health symptoms, family and friends rally around one another in their time of need.

Both Amy and Rosie work in care-centric careers. Amy works for child welfare services, talking to rebellious teens and moms struggling to regain custody of their children. Rosie is a social worker who talks with patients in hospitals and conducts wellness checks. Both show up for their charges many times over, sometimes coping with a runaway patient or a stubborn client who only wants the world to leave them to their lonely struggle. But time and again, the women show up with equal empathy for every grump and scared charge.

The emotional nature of these jobs and the loose, comfortable feel of time-tested relationships make up the foundation of Leigh’s script. One moment, a friend needs an ear to bitch about a bad day, the next it’s the other friend who needs a shoulder to cry on. The bond between Amy and Rosie feels rooted in years of traded secrets and jokes, while the cross-generational care between parents and child, shown through Amy and her family, comes across not in big, showy meltdowns or tearful screaming matches but in life pouring out between afternoon tea and evening glasses of wine. Conversation flows just as freely, yet the scenes are so structured that Tender Loving Care almost sounds like a play. Giving it a bit more cinematic flair, Leigh makes subtle work out of close-up shots, which means there’s no mistaking how his characters are feeling.

In both big and small ways, showing up for one another is one of life’s great responsibilities. To see these gentle acts of love so wonderfully captured by Leigh and his cast is a remarkable treat. Each member of the ensemble has their moment to shine and steal a few laughs (or tears), like returning Mr. Turner actors Bailey and Jesson do well. But of the ensemble, O’Flynn and Bailey Johnson stand out as they shoulder many of the movie’s most vulnerable moments with virtuoso performances. Finding incredible actors and giving them the material and space to feel through every conflicted note, to stifle the sobs of fully living in the role, has been one of Leigh’s hallmarks throughout his career. If Tender Loving Care does end up as Leigh’s swan song, it’s a perfectly heartfelt note to end on, right up to its final stirring close-up.
Starring: Kate O’Flynn, Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson, Alice Bailey Johnson
